lauridsen2019_single_gateway_lorawan_mod.note: arXiv 1912.01285. ⚠️ The CLOSEST CALL in the corpus, and adjudicated NONE on the protocol's stated criterion. Five hits: three are the LoRaWAN protocol's `repetitions` parameter (m, h) and one is ns-3 EXECUTION TIME ('each ns-3 simulation run takes tens of seconds'), all false positives. The fifth is real but insufficient: 'the positions of the nodes are randomly picked at each simulation run' tells a reader that runs vary WITHOUT giving a count, CI or dispersion -- none of the four things H1 names. Recorded in fairness: they DO publish their implementation so readers 'can easily replicate the results', which is better practice than most of the corpus, and is simply not the quantity being measured.

titolara2025_lorawan_80211ah_interferenc.note: Sensors 2025, DOI 10.3390/s25226924, via Europe PMC. ⚠️ THE MOST INSTRUCTIVE CASE IN THE CORPUS, and the one that proves H1 is about REPORTING and not about practice (protocol §1). They state their replication information completely: 'we fix the NS-3 random seed at runtime --seed=1; all reported results correspond to a single run per scenario', 'Each configuration was executed once (R = 1)', and 'the figures report the single-run outcome ... (no averaging across repetitions and no confidence intervals)'. Verdict REPORTS: a reader can judge the evidence exactly, and what they learn is that there is one run. Scoring this NONE because we dislike R=1 would silently convert H1 from a reporting claim into a practice claim, which §1 forbids in terms.
